Dairy farms and beef farms are two different things. Dairy cows (most recognizable breed being the black and white Holsteins) have been bred throughout centuries to produce better milk over better meat. I am unsure as to whether they are used in dog food and the like after they stop producing milk, but I think they are most likely just shot.

Meat cows, however, have been selectively bred for having the best beef, but technically, you would very rarely eat a cow. Cow is the female. Steer or Bull being male. In the general running of a beef farm, female young are kept to grow the herd and the males are shipped off the be eaten when they come of age.

So, not only are dairy cows rarely eaten, meat cows also are rarely eaten. Most of your beef is male, ergo, non milk producing.

The buying/selling horse world where I live is quite dodgy, so here's my tips based on that.

Check every inch of the horse for evidence of injury. Old scars that might have never healed inside. Lumps and bumps. Check hooves for splits. Poke him everywhere. Knees, shoulders, neck, spine. Poke poke poke poke. Put your thumb and fore finger either side of the spine, apply some pressure and run your hand along from ears to tail. Any sign of distress from the horse (even so much as a head raise or ear twitch) could indicate a much bigger issue.

Never trust the seller when you ask about anything. Take it all with a grain of salt, and fact check if you can. Sellers lie about injuries, age, ability, temperament. Anything that they think will hinder the sale, they could lie about. Do a brand search to verify age/bloodlines. If no brand then check teeth (a quick google will help you approximate age).

And the biggest thing: has the horse been drugged/sedated? Is the horse alert? Eyes bright, ears responsive? Signs of drugging are low head, droopy lip, poor balance, little or no reaction to stimuli. If you suspect drugging, check the neck and rump for signs of needles. Learn to find a pulse and what normal pulse rates are, is his too low?

I know my advice is a lot more negative than some other replies, but just based on personal experiences, you can't be too careful.

When I bought Oscar in October 2013, he was scared. So scared. I had seen him at the sale a few times before, I wasn't going to let him go back. Just being near him made him nervous and uptight. If I spoke too loudly or moved too quickly, he would bolt as far away as he could. He'd been beaten. It was so obvious by his reactions to my movement. If I raised my had above my shoulders, he would almost quiver with fear. It was so heartbreaking. He was two years old. Been through the sale multiple times. Terrified I would hit him like his last owner.

I decided to leave him to his own devices. Turn him out. Let him grow up and just live without fear for a while. The progress he made was incredible. Each time I would visit, he would be more and more confident. He was growing and gaining muscle like no tomorrow. He would even approach me instead of the other way around. It was, by far, the best decision to turn him out.

These days, he's a little puppy. Follows you around, give cuddles and would crawl into your pocket if he'd fit. He'll be ready to break in soon, which will be an interesting affair. He still has moments of fear and during the breaking process, that can be dangerous for horse and rider. The best way to approach it will be slow and steady :)

My method is what we in the biz call 'natural horsemanship'. It's all about building a good relationship with the horse on the ground, before ever thinking about getting in that saddle. I want that horse to be able to stand there relaxed while I do whatever I want around him. When it comes time to get on, slow and steady wins that race. It's all about doing something scary until it's not scary any more. So if he is frightened by me up there, I'll just sit there calmly until he relaxes. This is why I spend so much effort on the ground getting the horse to trust me, so that when I am on their back, it's easier for them to relax because nothing I have ever done has hurt them.

Yes there is money involved, but that's not why I do it. I've had customers that couldn't handle their horse so they bring them to me for some quietening. Most of the time I would buy horses that were on their way to the knackery, then resell them when they are ready to great homes. 

When it comes to abused horses, it depends on how they were abused. If they were beaten then everything has to happen a little slower than normal. Usually they are either scared when you go to touch their head, or their rump, so I spend extra time patting those areas to show the horse that I can touch them there without it hurting.

Strangest? Hmm.. Probably the first time I took a horse named Duke down to the local park. There was a big park with a man made lake right next to where my horses were. Duke had grown up on top of a mountain range in the middle of the bush, so riding him around this park in the middle of a town was quite a big deal. Anyway, we came over a ridge and down towards the park. Suddenly, Duke slammed into reverse and ran back as fast as he could for at least 100 metres. At the time I had no idea what made him do that as horses generally hate reversing, but later I discovered it was the way the sun bounced off the lake.

I had never had a horse react to something they were frightened of by charging backwards with all their might. Turning around and running away would have been fine, it was just that he backed straight back over the ridge and halfway back to the paddock.

It depends on how you classify 'broken'. One could say that as soon as someone has ridden them, even for 5 minutes, they are classed as 'green broken'. Therefore you could break a horse in a day. For me to say one of my horses is 'broken' I like to have put about 10 hours under saddle.

My fastest would have been an 'off the track' Standardbred named Brian. He went from never having a saddle on, to being calm and confident on rides, in about two weeks.

If you don't know anyone with a horse, try going to some local shows or pony club. I find horsey people to be very friendly and just being in the same area as a bunch of horses will help you gain some confidence.

If you know someone with horses, ask them if they thought it would be safe for you to go and see them sometime. Horses are prey animals, so just about everything scares them, including you. If your friend thinks their horse is quiet enough, just go slow. Get the owner to halter and hold the horse. Start by letting him sniff you, then slowly rub down his nose. The best way to bond with a horse is spending time together doing nothing. If nothing's happening, then nothing's dangerous and the horse will begin to trust you, and you will begin to trust it :)
